item.title: St. John's Episcopal Church in Franklin, Pennsylvania
item.description:
Nestled on a quiet back street in the once-booming oil town of Franklin, PA, sits St. John's Episcopal Church. While the exterior is pleasing and well-maintained, the true treasures are discovered once you pass through the large wood-and-iron doors. 

Every window at St. John's was created by the studios of Louis Comfort Tiffany! Furthermore, St. John's is one of only seven remaining churches with a complete collection of Tiffany windows. 

The main sanctuary houses a Rose Window (the 3rd largest ever created by Tiffany Studios) as well as a series of triptychs depicting the life of Christ. Beyond the windows, there are other interesting architectural highlights to take in, like the rare rosewood pews and two detailed mosaics created by Gorham Art Studio.

You can visit the windows Tuesdays through Fridays from 8 AM to 2 PM. If you'd like a guided tour, please call the church office to arrange it at least one week before your visit. Guided tours cost $5 per person, with a maximum group size of 50.

item.title: 8 Gargoyles and Grotesques Hiding in Plain Sight
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
What’s more wondrous than towering spires on a building? Stained glass? Vaulted windows, or garden roofs? One word: Ghouls. Nothing jazzes up a normal old cathedral or mansion more than a mischievous face etched in stone, smiling (or, more likely, grimacing) at those passing below. Gargoyles and grotesques, in their own endearingly ugly way, are one of the best ways for architects to let their creations stand apart from the pack and inspire reflection for centuries to come.

While most of these creatures are made in a similar style, with recognizable bodily features, expressions, and poses, there are a handful around the globe that are unapologetically unique: sometimes familiar, sometimes offbeat, and always worth a closer look.

A Note on Gargoyles vs. Grotesques

Both are ornate stone figures carved into buildings; however, gargoyles also double as waterspouts to drain rainwater off a building, whereas grotesques are purely decorative.


1. Darth Vader Grotesque - Washington, D.C.

D.C.’s National Cathedral is the largest in the U.S. and the sixth largest in the world, but it has another, less obvious claim to fame: a small carving of Darth Vader among its spires. When the cathedral underwent constuction in the 1980s, it held a contest for schoolchildren to submit designs, and this infamous villain took third place, earning it a spot on the exterior. For the best view of the Dark Lord, grab your binoculars and head to the northwest parking lot. Near the top of the northwest tower, Vader is just above a large skull.

2. House with Chimaeras - Kyiv, Ukraine

Polish-Ukrainian architect Vladislav Gorodetsky, “the Gaudí, of Ukraine,” intended for this animal-themed building to be his permanent residence; however, he was forced to vacate it when his pocketbook ran dry. The house, located in Kyiv’s historic Lypky neighborhood, is right across the street from the Ukrainian president’s office and has been used for diplomatic ceremonies since 2005. Its gargoyles and grotesques were inspired by Gorodetsky’s love of hunting, and inside is even filled with stuffed versions of many of these same animals.

3. Plein Rond de Eik - Amersfoort, Netherlands

Architect Changiz Tehrani designed this mixed-use structure with 22 different WhatsApp emoji faces that stare out at passersby, including fan favorites like the smile, the wink, the heart eyes, the kissy face, and the winking face with tongue out. Tehrani drew inspiration from an Amsterdam building called “The House with the Heads,” which depicts the faces of six Greek gods.

4. The Policeman Grotesque - Carlisle, England

An officer who died in the line of duty is memorialized on the south-facing outer wall of Carlisle Cathedral, surprisingly inconspicuous beside the medieval gargoyles and grotesques. Police Constable George Russell’s stone likeness wears a helmet and star badge, marking his life’s dedication to service and safety. Russell is buried in Carlisle and also honored by a plaque at the Oxenholme Lake District railway station.

5. The Bull of Santa Maria del Fiore - Florence, Italy

Among the Duomo’s many easy-to-miss intricacies is this stone bull’s head facing Via Ricasoli and right over the Porta della mandorla, the door that allows one up into the grand dome. There are two explanations for the bull’s origin: One holds that it was the builders’ tribute to the draft animals used to construct the cathedral. The other (far more fun) theory is that a stonemason designed the bull to look straight into the shop of his girlfriend’s husband, a daily reminder that it was the stonemason she truly loved.

6. The Vampire Rabbit of Newcastle - Newcastle upon Tyne, England

For over a century, this deformed rabbit has sat at the back of St. Nicholas Cathedral, but no one can say why or how it came to be. Some say it represents the coming of spring (à la the Easter Bunny), whereas others insist it was built to scare away grave robbers. Still others believe the creature was intended to be a normal rabbit but, unfortunately, its ears were accidentally put on backward.

7. ‘Alien’ Gargoyle - Paisley, Scotland

When Paisley Abbey underwent renovations in 1993, 13 of its gargoyles were removed and replaced with updated versions, though one of the stonemasons on the job took some major creative liberties. His contribution to the facade looks strikingly like H.R. Giger's Xenomorph from the “Alien” franchise, though it’s never been confirmed whether this was his exact intention or a happy coincidence.

8. Park Grove Manor - Oak Park, Illinois

E.E. Roberts designed a number of homes in this sleepy Chicago suburb, working in styles that ranged from Victorian to Tudor to Prairie. Perhaps his most fanciful building, Park Grove Manor is adorned with playful, chubby-faced gargoyles and grotesques. Above the service entrances to the building are sculptures depicting an architect and a bricklayer, both of them amusingly cartoonish. This may have been Roberts becoming less self-serious in his older age, joyfully deriding the pretensions of modern architecture.

item.title: Frank & Nancy’s Marine Corps Museum in De Pere, Wisconsin
item.description:
Frank Cornelius, a retired Korea and Vietnam War veteran has taken what started out as a personal collection of Marine Corps memorabilia and created a museum, with his wife Nancy. He gives guided tours (by appointment) during the summer months.  

The collection started out as a display in the family basement but outgrew that space. After moving the display to another building, it has grown impressively, thanks to generous donations from private individuals. Walk along with Frank as he recounts the history and tells tales of days gone by. Many of the items are from his own service in the Marines, which lasted 22 years.

The Marine Corps Museum is truly a labor of love and a testament to service.

item.title: Giant Squid Museum in Luarca, Spain
item.description:
Forget the kraken of sailors’ nightmares. The monster really does exist—and in the Asturian fishing town of Luarca, you can come face-to-face with one. Far from being a ship-swallowing beast, the giant squid is a mysterious inhabitant of the ocean depths whose strange anatomy has inspired legends for centuries.

Known scientifically as Architeuthis, the giant squid can reach around 20 meters in length and weigh up to a ton. It has three hearts, enormous eyes adapted to the darkness of the abyss, eight arms, two feeding tentacles, and a formidable parrot-like beak. Although found worldwide, these elusive creatures appear with unusual frequency off the Asturian coast, particularly around the deep Carrandi fishing grounds and the Avilés Canyon.

The Giant Squid Museum in Luarca, Asturias has survived a watery encounter worthy of its exhibits. Its original home on Luarca’s harbor was devastated by a severe sea storm on February 2, 2014, when enormous waves flooded and destroyed its lower floors. After remaining closed for eight years, the museum reopened in a new, more sheltered location. Today, six giant squid are displayed alongside other deep-sea specimens, while atmospheric lighting, underwater sounds, interactive exhibits, and an anatomy laboratory recreate the eerie world they inhabit. Among the highlights is a 176-kilogram female accidentally caught in 2015. Here, the legendary kraken becomes something even stranger: a real animal that still has plenty of secrets left to reveal.
